Message safety
This warning is based on signals found locally on your device. It does not prove that the sender is malicious, but it is a reason to verify the request before you act.
Detected reasons
Safety signals Sparrow can detect

Links can lead to fake sign-in, payment, or download pages. Sparrow may flag a link when its destination or structure looks unusual or deceptive. Before opening it, verify the sender and inspect the destination carefully. If the message asks you to sign in, pay, or confirm sensitive information, open the service from its official app or a trusted bookmark instead of using the link in the message.

A lookalike domain is written to resemble a trusted website while actually pointing somewhere else. Attackers may replace letters with similar characters, add extra words or hyphens, or place a familiar brand name inside an unrelated domain. Check the registered domain itself, not only the part of the address that looks familiar.

Some characters from Cyrillic, Greek, and other writing systems can look almost identical to Latin letters. A malicious address can mix these character sets so that a fake domain appears to be a familiar one. Treat links with unexpected character combinations cautiously and open the service through a trusted route instead.

This link points directly to a numeric IP address instead of a recognizable domain name. That is legitimate in some technical environments, but in unsolicited messages it can hide which organization actually operates the destination. Avoid entering credentials or payment information unless you independently know and trust the address.

URL shorteners replace the real destination with a short redirect link. This can be convenient, but it also prevents you from seeing where the link will ultimately take you before you open it. Be especially careful when a shortened link is combined with an urgent request, a login request, or a payment request.

The message uses urgency, threats, deadlines, or pressure to make you act before you can verify the situation. Common examples include claims that an account will be locked, a payment must be made immediately, or an opportunity will disappear. Slow down and confirm the request independently before following instructions.

The message asks for information that could give someone access to an account, such as a password, PIN, authentication code, verification code, or other login data. Legitimate services should not require you to send these secrets in a chat. Do not share them, and use the service's official app or website if you need to check your account.

The message asks you to transfer money, buy gift cards, send cryptocurrency, or complete another payment. Payment requests become more suspicious when they are unexpected, urgent, or use new account details. Verify unusual requests with the sender through a separate trusted channel before paying.

Private keys, recovery phrases, seed phrases, and similar secrets can provide complete control over an account, identity, or wallet. A legitimate support agent or contact should never need you to send them in a message. Never share these secrets. If one has already been disclosed, treat it as compromised and replace or revoke it where possible.
